# Medication for Parkinson disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Relevant pharmacology > Medication for Parkinson disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/Zm0ZVg)

---

## Summary

There are many pharmacologic options available for the treatment of <u>Parkinson disease</u>; regimens are tailored to the patient's age, symptoms, and symptom severity. While only symptomatic treatment is available at this point in time, drugs that may slow or reverse the course of the disease are currently being investigated. Since treatment of <u>Parkinson disease</u> at an early stage can significantly improve a patient's subjective well-being (honeymoon period), medical therapy should be initiated as soon as symptoms begin to interfere with the patient's daily life. For most patients, first-line treatment consists of <u>levodopa</u> (<u>L-DOPA</u>) or <u>dopamine receptor agonists</u>, e.g., <u>ropinirole</u> and <u>pramipexole</u>. Other drugs that are used to treat <u>Parkinson disease</u> include <u>amantadine</u>, <u>MAO-B inhibitors</u>, and <u>COMT inhibitors</u>.

| Decarboxylase inhibitors |  | <br><br>* Carbidopa<br><br>* Benserazide<br><br><br> | <br>* Blockage of <u>DOPA decarboxylase</u> → ↓ peripheral conversion of <u>L-DOPA</u> to <u>dopamine</u> →↑ <u>bioavailability</u> and ↓ peripheral side effects of <u>L-DOPA</u> (e.g., <u>orthostatic hypotension</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Always administered alongside <u>L-DOPA</u><br><br> |  |  |  |
| <br>Dopamine agonists<br> | Non-ergot | <br><br>* Ropinirole<br><br>* Pramipexole<br><br>* Apomorphine<br><br>* Rotigotine<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Act directly at striatal <u>dopamine</u> <u>receptors</u><br><br>* Predominantly control <u>bradykinetic</u> symptoms<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Initial treatment option for PD, especially in younger patients<br><br>* Adjunctive treatment for patients of any age<br><br>* Second-line treatment for <u>restless leg syndrome</u><br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>orthostatic hypotension</u>, <u>daytime drowsiness</u><br><br>* <u>Hallucinations</u>, <u>psychosis</u>, <u>impulse control disorders</u> (may be mistaken for an acute <u>manic episode</u>)<br><br>* <u>Dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Ergot dopamine agonists</u>: <u>fibrosis</u> (cardial, pleural, <u>retroperitoneal</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Less effective than <u>L-DOPA</u>, but fewer motor side effects<br><br>* Effective in advanced disease stages<br><br><br> |
| Ergot | <br>* Bromocriptine<br><br> | <br>* No longer recommended for treatment of PD<br><br> |  |  |  |  |  |
| COMT inhibitors |  | <br><br>* Entacapone<br><br>* Tolcapone<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Inhibition of <u>catechol-O-methyltransferase</u> (<u>COMT</u>) → ↓ peripheral metabolization of <u>L-DOPA</u> to 3-O-<u>methyldopa</u> (3-OMD) → ↑ availability<br><br>* <u>Tolcapone</u> also prevents central <u>COMT</u> from breaking down <u>dopamine</u> to 3-methoxytyramine (3-MT) by crossing the <u>blood-brain</u> barrier → ↑ <u>dopamine</u> effect → ↓ demand for <u>L-DOPA</u> and longer therapeutic effect for each dose<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Entacapone</u>: If <u>L-DOPA</u> loses effect or motor symptoms fluctuate during <u>L-DOPA</u> therapy<br><br>* <u>Tolcapone</u>: for refractory <u>Parkinson disease</u><br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* Gastrointestinal side effects<br><br>* <u>Dyskinesia</u> and psychiatric symptoms (e.g., <u>hallucinations</u> or confusion)<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>COMT inhibitor</u> monotherapy is ineffective; therefore, it should always be combined with <u>L-DOPA</u> and <u>carbidopa</u>.<br><br> |
| NMDA antagonists |  | <br>* <u>Amantadine</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Acts antagonistically at the <u>glutamate</u> N-methyl-D-aspartate <u>(NMDA) receptor</u> → <u>dopaminergic</u> effect<br><br>* ↑ <u>Dopamine</u> release and ↓ <u>dopamine</u> reuptake in central <u>neurons</u><br><br>* Mostly controls <u>bradykinetic</u> symptoms<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Short-term treatment of mild symptoms<br><br>* Drug of choice during <u>akinetic crisis</u><br><br>* Reduction of <u>L-DOPA</u>-induced <u>dyskinesia</u><br><br><br> |  | <br>* Similar to <u>L-DOPA</u> (less pronounced), including:<br><br>* <u>Ataxia</u><br><br>* <u>Livedo reticularis</u><br><br>* <u>Peripheral edema</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Loss of effect after several months of treatment → cannot be used for long-term therapy<br><br>* May have cardiac side effects (prolonged <u>QT interval</u>)<br><br><br> |
| MAO-B inhibitors |  | <br><br>* Rasagiline<br><br>* Safinamide<br><br>* Selegiline<br><br><br> | <br>* Selective inhibition of <u>MAO</u>-B → ↓ metabolization of <u>dopamine</u> into <u>DOPAC</u> in the <u>brain</u>  → prolonged <u>dopamine</u> availability and effect→ ↓ demand for <u>L-DOPA</u><br><br> | <br>* Alternative to <u>L-DOPA</u> or <u>dopamine agonists</u> for short-term therapy in patients with mild symptoms in early disease stages<br><br> |  | <br>* <u>Headache</u>, <u>dyskinesia</u>, psychological disorders (e.g., <u>hallucinations</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Can also be given in combination with <u>L-DOPA</u> → ↓ motor fluctuations<br><br> |
| <u>Anticholinergic drugs</u><br>(<u>muscarinic antagonists</u>) |  | <br><br>* Benztropine<br><br>* Trihexyphenidyl<br><br>* Biperiden<br><br><br> | <br>* Inhibition of excitatory cholinergic <u>neurons</u> → ↓ concentration of <u>acetylcholine</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Useful as monotherapy in patients < 65 years of age with <u>tremor</u> as the main symptom<br><br>* Beneficial regarding <u>tremor</u> and rigidity but does not improve <u>bradykinesia</u><br><br><br> |  | <br>* See “<u>Antimuscarinic side effects</u>” for details.<br><br> | <br>* Usually avoided in patients > 65 years because they are more <u>prone</u> to <u>anticholinergic side effects</u> (e.g., <u>urinary retention</u>, <u>delirium</u>, <u>constipation</u>)<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> Patients who do not respond to <u>levodopa</u> therapy will not respond to <u>dopamine agonist</u> therapy!




> [!NOTE]
> Selegiline has high selectivity for the <u>monoamine oxidase</u> B found predominantly in the brain.




> [!NOTE]
> To remember that <u>anticholinergics</u> like benztropine and trihexyphenidyl are used in the treatment of Parkinson disease, think of “A Benz for a trip to the park.”




> [!NOTE]
> To remember the main drugs used to treat <u>Parkinson disease</u>, think of A<sup>2</sup>B<sup>2</sup>C<sup>2</sup>D<sup>2</sup>: Antimuscarinics and Amantadine; Bromocriptine and <u>MAO</u>-B inhibitors; COMT inhibitors and Carbidopa; L-D<u>OPA</u> and <u>nonergot</u> Dopamine <u>agonists</u>.

## Adverse effects

### Carbidopa-levodopa




* Becomes less effective over time: may require a shorter interval between doses

* Autonomic symptoms

* <u>Nausea</u> and <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Orthostatic hypotension</u>

* <u>Carbidopa</u> reduces the risk of <u>orthostatic hypotension</u>, <u>nausea</u>, and <u>vomiting</u>.

* Psychiatric symptoms [[6]](/library/xsaECN)[[7]](/library/BsazCN)

* <u>Hallucinations</u> (often visual);   and other <u>psychotic symptoms</u> → treat with <u>clozapine</u>

* <u>Anxiety</u>, <u>insomnia</u>, <u>agitation</u>, and aggressive behavior

* Increased risk in elderly patients, women, concurrent <u>dementia</u> or other psychiatric disorders (e.g., <u>depression</u>), long duration of <u>levodopa</u> treatment, and high doses

* Motor fluctuations 

* Hypokinesia

* End-of-dose akinesia/<u>wearing-off phenomenon</u>

* Freezing

* On-off phenomenon; : Phases of good mobility (“on” phases) alternate with phases of poor mobility (“off” phases) as a result of reduced reaction to <u>L-DOPA</u> or <u>wearing off</u> of medication.

* Dyskinesia (hyperkinesia)

* On-period dystonia

* Off-period dystonia

* Diphasic dyskinesias

* Increased <u>intraocular pressure</u>

* <u>Open-angle glaucoma</u>: <u>Levodopa</u> (and <u>anticholinergics</u>) should be used with caution.

* <u>Closed-angle glaucoma</u>: <u>Levodopa</u> (and <u>anticholinergics</u>) are not recommended.

* Akinetic crisis

* Definition: condition caused by severe <u>dopamine</u> deficiency (e.g., after discontinuation of <u>L-DOPA</u> therapy or insufficient <u>L-DOPA</u> absorption)

* Clinical features: complete inability to move , incomprehensible speech, possibly <u>hyperthermia</u> → increased risk of <u>dehydration</u>, deep-<u>vein</u> <u>thrombosis</u>, and <u>pneumonia</u>

* Treatment: intensive medical care, volume substitution, administration of <u>L-DOPA</u>, <u>apomorphine</u>, <u>amantadine</u>





![Akinetic crisis](media/dlim27b3kekz5cb5b8imspyf.jpg)

Akinetic crisis




### <u>Dopamine agonists</u>




#### Side effects common to all <u>dopamine agonists</u>




* Autonomic

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Orthostatic hypotension</u>, <u>dizziness</u>

* Increased <u>daytime drowsiness</u>, <u>sleep</u> attacks

* <u>Motor function</u>: <u>dyskinesia</u> (rare)

* Psychiatric [[6]](/library/xsaECN)[[7]](/library/BsazCN)

* <u>Hallucinations</u>, <u>psychosis</u>

* <u>Impulse control disorders</u>

* Manifestations: e.g., <u>pathological gambling</u>, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping

* Management: dose reduction or discontinuation until symptoms resolve

* Unrest, confusion

* Dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome

* Etiology: abrupt discontinuation of <u>dopamine agonist</u> therapy

* Clinical features: similar to <u>malignant hyperthermia</u> and <u>neuroleptic malignant syndrome</u> → <u>hyperthermia</u> and <u>rigor</u>; <u>akinesia</u>; reduced vigilance; increased <u>creatine kinase</u> levels, <u>transaminases</u>, and <u>leukocytes</u>

* Treatment: intensive medical care, volume substitution, administration of <u>L-DOPA</u>, <u>apomorphine</u>, <u>amantadine</u>





#### Side effects of <u>ergotamine</u>-derived <u>agonists</u> (e.g., <u>bromocriptine</u>)



* <u>Fibrosis</u> (cardiac <u>fibrosis</u>, <u>Raynaud disease</u>, pleural <u>pulmonary fibrosis</u>, and <u>retroperitoneal fibrosis</u>)




### Other substances




* <u>NMDA antagonists</u> (<u>amantadine</u>): side effects are similar to <u>L-DOPA</u> but much less pronounced

* <u>Ataxia</u>

* <u>Livedo reticularis</u>

* <u>Peripheral edema</u>

* <u>MAO-B inhibitors</u>

* <u>Headache</u>, <u>dyskinesia</u>, psychological disorders (e.g., <u>hallucinations</u>)

* Inhibition of <u>MAO</u>-A with higher doses  → reduced peripheral <u>degradation of catecholamines</u> → adrenergic side effects (e.g., <u>tachycardia</u>, sweating, nervousness)

* <u>Muscarinic antagonists</u> (<u>anticholinergics</u>): See “<u>Antimuscarinic side effects</u>.”

* <u>COMT inhibitors</u>

* Gastrointestinal side effects

* <u>Dyskinesia</u> and psychiatric symptoms (e.g., <u>hallucinations</u> or confusion)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>NMDA antagonists</u> can cause prolonged <u>QT intervals</u>! Do not administer <u>NMDA antagonists</u> to patients with a history of cardiac disorders!




> [!WARNING]
> Administration of <u>antimuscarinic drugs</u> to patients with mental disorders or <u>delirium</u> will likely worsen psychiatric symptoms!




We list the most important adverse effects. The selection is not exhaustive.
